paper.title: CoCoDA: Co-evolving Compositional DAG for Tool-Augmented Agents
paper.central_claim: A single compositional code DAG (typed signature, description, pre/post spec, examples per tool) lets a small planner and its tool library co-evolve: Typed DAG Retrieval keeps prompt cost sublinear in library size, validated composite tools are folded from successful trajectories by a fixed teacher, and a DAG-induced saved-call reward trains the planner with GRPO; an 8B student matches or exceeds a 32B teacher on GSM8K and MATH and beats tool-use and library-learning baselines.

evidence.quote: Tool-augmented language models can extend small language models with external executable skills, but scaling the tool library creates a coupled challenge: the library must evolve with the planner as new reusable subroutines emerge, while retrieval from the growing library must remain within a fixed context budget. Existing tool-use and skill-library methods typically treat tools as flat or text-indexed memories, causing prompt cost to grow with library size and obscuring the typed, compositional structure of executable code. We propose CoCoDA, a framework that co-evolves the planner and tool library through a single code-native structure: a compositional code DAG. Nodes are primitive or composite tools, edges encode invocation dependencies, and each node stores a typed signature, description, pre/post-condition specification, and worked examples. At inference time, Typed DAG Retrieval prunes candidates by symbolic signature unification, ranks survivors by descriptions, filters them by behavioral specifications, and disambiguates with examples, keeping expensive context materialization on progressively smaller candidate sets. At training time, successful trajectories are folded into validated composite tools, while the planner is updated with a DAG-induced reward that credits composites by their primitive expansion size. We provide theoretical results showing retrieval cost reduction, sublinear retrieval time, compositional advantage under the shaped reward, monotone co-evolution under conservative updates, and DAG well-formedness. Across mathematical reasoning, tabular analysis, and code task benchmarks, CoCoDA enables an 8B student to match or exceed a 32B teacher on GSM8K and MATH and consistently improves over strong tool-use and library-learning baselines.
evidence.support_explanation: Original central claim: typed executable DAG jointly supports retrieval, growth and rewards; theoretical sublinearity/monotonicity and8B-vs32Bmath results claimed.

evidence.quote:
This section addresses axes (A) and (C) of Eq. (1). Typed DAG Retrieval is coarse-to-fine along two orthogonal axes. The first is the
abstraction axis
induced by the compositional DAG: retrieval starts from the highest-level tool whose signature can cover the current subgoal and descends to children only when that composite is too broad, incompatible, or insufficiently discriminative. Thus, the retriever stops as soon as a validated composite can solve the subgoal, instead of blindly opening all lower-level subskills. The second is the
evidence axis
inside each candidate node: compatibility is judged using increasingly informative and increasingly expensive records, from typed signatures to descriptions, specifications, and examples. These two axes play different roles. The abstraction axis decides
how deep
retrieval must go in the executable skill DAG, while the evidence axis decides
which alternative implementation
at the current abstraction level should be surfaced.

The key asymmetry is that tool compatibility becomes increasingly expensive to judge. Type compatibility is symbolic; semantic relevance requires description ranking; behavioral compatibility requires contract checking; and fine-grained disambiguation requires examples. CoCoDA orders these checks from cheapest to most expensive and pays each expensive cost only on the survivors of earlier stages.

assessment.strongest_supported_claim: A teacher-built, typed executable tool DAG co-trained with a GRPO planner gives small, consistent test-accuracy gains (about 0.5-2 points) over a fixed-inventory RL tool-use baseline at four student sizes, and the cascade retrieval is much cheaper than flat retrieval at large library sizes (author-reported, 3 seeds).

G.reason: Opus = son55. Growing a library with the planner is a real problem, and the lineage is broad. But the motivating context-budget bottleneck does not bind in the regime the method produces: the trained libraries are 205–382 tools (Table 5), accuracy plateaus by about 400, and the 1,600-node regime is never reached by training (opus:O04). The 'never both' missing quadrant is the paper's own taxonomy (run precedent: H-Mem). Most named neighbours (Voyager, CRAFT, ReGAL, DreamCoder/Stitch) are not compared.

M.reason: Opus = sol. The design (typed cascade, teacher-folded composites, saved-call reward) is concrete, but its stated justification is invalid in key places. Theorem 1 derives o(C_flat) from limsup ≤ α1α2 < 1, and L2 still ranks all α1·n L1 survivors (sol:E028, sol:E004). Corollary 5's log-depth argument fails on a chain (sol:E031). Theorem 4's library step treats LLM-judged L3 checks as certified equivalence, with 'no false positives under faithful reading' (sol:E005, sol:E030). The saved-call reward can credit unnecessary composites, which the authors concede for large λ (sol:E007, sol:E025). Mechanism plausible, key assumptions weak.

X.reason: Opus = sol. Algorithms 1–3, prompts and Table 4 are given, but the retention mechanism cannot be reconstructed as reported. The admission threshold ρ acts on a binary R_res ∈ {0,1} (Table 4), yet the ρ sweep reports 419/364/207 retained composites at 0.5/0.8/1.0, which is impossible on fixed binary rewards (sol:E019, sol:E026). Child-spec validation and dedup are LLM prompts. The EvalPlus query stream is undefined (opus:O05). There is no retirement, versioning or rollback.

E.measurement.reason: Shared-error correction (both seats 3). The verifiers are standard and deterministic, but the reported numbers do not reconcile. (1) Table 2's Δ column ≠ the mean of its cells (−1.97 vs −1.79, −4.46 vs −4.64, −5.01 vs −5.18; opus:O01). (2) The appendix equates the all-off variant with a ReTool-style planner, yet it sits 3–5 pts below ReTool (son55:E012). (3) Tool counts disagree: 1,873 vs 309, and 42 vs 14–22 primitives (son55:E020). (4) The 'upper bound' teacher is tool-free CoT. Run convention: contradictions cap at 2.

E.causality.reason: Both seats 2, confirmed. ReTool (frozen inventory, same RL backbone) is the intended co-evolution control: CoCoDA is ahead in all 24 cells, but by 0.1–1.6 pts against SDs ≤0.4–0.7, and parity (teacher SFT, tool inventory, steps) is unstated. The component ablations are internally inconsistent with that control (all-off ≪ ReTool). w/o CTD also zeroes the reward. There is no static-library arm, and they cover 4B only.

E.holdout.reason: Opus = sol. Five benchmarks use official train/test splits, with the library and planner built on training streams. Not 3, for two reasons. (1) EvalPlus has no training split, but an EvalPlus library was evolved from an undefined stream (opus:O05). (2) λ and k2 were selected on test accuracy: Table 8's λ = 0.20 value equals the Table 1 test score, and there is no validation split (opus:O02, opus:O03). The sensitivity in [0.1, 0.3] is ≤0.6 pts, so the bias is small but real. There is no leakage guard.

E.statistics.reason: Both seats 2, confirmed (A2 tier 2). Three named seeds with SD upper bounds (≤0.4 / ≤0.7) in prose. There are no per-cell SDs, CIs or tests, and the ablations have no SD. Several ReTool margins (e.g. 0.11 at 4B WTQ/FinQA) are below the stated SD bound.

E.cost.reason: Opus = sol. CoCoDA's stage wall-clock and GPU-hours (35–98) and the retrieval-token ratios (11.4×/4.7× at 1,600 nodes) are reported. The teacher-call cost, the baselines' training cost and any matched-budget comparison are absent, and the token-ratio regime is not one training produces (opus:O04).
